name: The AI Pilot Acceptance Checklist
short: Before the pilot becomes the process.
description: Six practical checks to make ownership, quality and the next decision explicit.
label: DECISION WORKSHEET
audience: Pilot sponsors, operations leaders and project owners
intro: A successful demonstration is not the same as a workflow your team can rely on. Use this worksheet to record the evidence, owners and open questions before deciding to expand. It is a decision aid, not a certification or a promise of return.
checks: A named owner
Who is accountable after the demonstration? Who can pause the workflow? Write down both the names and the responsibilities.
A measured baseline
What is the current task volume, completion time and correction effort? Separate measured inputs from assumptions.
A quality threshold
What makes an output usable? Include examples that should be accepted, rejected or escalated. Test difficult cases as well as the happy path.
Human review and exceptions
What must a person approve? How do exceptions reach them? How can the original process be restored?
Access and maintenance
Which information is needed? Who can access it? Who maintains the sources and integration? Include your organisation’s security and privacy review where relevant.
A commercial decision
Compare observed benefits with software, implementation, review and maintenance costs. Agree what evidence means expand, revise or stop.
closing: Do not turn six unanswered questions into one reassuring score. Record the evidence for each, name the remaining owners, then make an explicit decision.

name: The AI Opportunity Canvas
description: A one-workflow canvas for choosing a useful, bounded next step.
label: WORKING CANVAS
audience: Leadership teams, internal champions and workflow owners
intro: Start with the work, not the tool. This canvas helps you define a specific task, the people involved and the conditions a useful improvement would have to meet. It is designed to open a good discussion, not generate an automatic recommendation.
fields: The decision we need to make
checks: Define the actual task
Describe the task in one sentence. What starts it, what finishes it, and who uses the result?
Find the friction
Where does time or attention go today? Include checking, copying, waiting, corrections and exceptions.
Map the information
What sources are needed? Are they accessible, current and approved for the intended use? Who owns them?
Describe a useful result
What would improve, and how would you recognise it? Keep the outcome separate from the features of a possible tool.
Set the boundaries
Which decisions stay with a person? What must not be automated? Consider a simpler process or conventional automation too.
Choose a small next step
Name the owner, the test, the evidence required and the date for a decision. What would make you continue, revise or stop?
closing: A useful opportunity has a real task, a responsible owner and a way to test the difference. It does not need to sound impressive.

name: The Team AI Readiness Guide
description: Understand the team’s starting point without reducing people to an AI score.
label: TEAM DISCUSSION GUIDE
audience: Team leaders, people teams and learning sponsors
intro: Before choosing training, understand how your team works today. Use these prompts with the people involved. Look for differences in access, confidence and context, not a score that ranks employees.
checks: Shared understanding
Can the team explain where AI could help and where it could be wrong? Which questions are people hesitant to ask?
Access and permissions
Do people know which tools they may use, with what information, and whom to ask when they are unsure?
Relevant tasks
Which recurring tasks would make useful practice? Choose work that matters and can be discussed safely.
Quality and judgement
How is work checked today? Can people recognise an answer that is plausible but unsuitable for its purpose?
Time and support
Is there room to practise between sessions? Who can help connect learning to everyday work?
Evidence of progress
What should people be able to do afterwards? Choose a few observable tasks and agree how to review them fairly.
closing: Use the gaps to shape the programme, not to judge the people. A shared starting point makes the learning more relevant and the follow-through more realistic.
